overview: In each annotation, you will see one original r/ChangeMyView post and two direct responses to that post, labeled Response A and Response B. You will make three judgments in this order: Cogency, Expected Rhetorical Effectiveness, and Evidential Support. Judge only the material shown to you. Do not search the web, use AI assistants, look up the users, or use information from later discussion. Base your judgments about the OP on the original post and reasonable inferences from what the OP says. Do not assume facts about the OP that are unsupported by the post or use outside information about the user. Judge each displayed pair on its own. Do not revisit an earlier answer merely to make your answers form a perfectly consistent ranking across all responses.
scale_intro: For Cogency and Expected Rhetorical Effectiveness, choose exactly one of four positions on the comparative scale: Strong A, Weak A, Weak B, or Strong B. Every position selects either A or B; the Strong/Weak distinction records how large the difference seems. Use Strong when one response is clearly better on the question being asked. Use Weak when one response is only somewhat better or you have only a slight preference. There is no tie option. If the responses seem nearly equal, choose the side you lean toward and use Weak. Strong/Weak describes the strength of the comparative preference, not your confidence in your own judgment. The same four-way scale appears for Evidential Support only when both responses are marked as providing evidence.

scale.Strong A: Response A is clearly better on the target question.
scale.Weak A: Response A is somewhat better, or you only slightly prefer A.
scale.Weak B: Response B is somewhat better, or you only slightly prefer B.
scale.Strong B: Response B is clearly better on the target question.

cogency.title: COGENCY — QUALITY OF THE ARGUMENT
cogency.full: A cogent argument offers reasons that adequately support its conclusion. Judge the argument advanced by the response itself. Consider three aspects: Acceptability — are the premises reasonable enough to serve as support for the conclusion? Relevance — do the premises actually bear on the conclusion? Sufficiency — taken together, do the premises provide enough support for drawing the conclusion? Do not judge cogency by whether you personally agree with the conclusion or by whether this particular OP is likely to be persuaded. Use the material shown and ordinary background knowledge. Do not conduct external fact-checking. A response does not need citations or formal evidence to be cogent.
cogency.short: Which response advances the more cogent argument? Consider whether its reasons are acceptable, relevant, and sufficient. Judge argument quality, not whether this particular OP would be persuaded.
cogency.question: Which response advances the more cogent argument?

effectiveness.title: EXPECTED RHETORICAL EFFECTIVENESS — LIKELIHOOD OF CHANGING THIS OP'S VIEW
effectiveness.full: Predict which response is more likely to change this particular OP's stated view. Use the original post to understand the OP's stated position, reasons, concerns, values, priorities, and other context they provide. You may make reasonable inferences from this information when predicting what might persuade them. In many cases, the OP will not explicitly state everything that matters, so use your best judgment based on the context available in the post. Do not assume unsupported personal characteristics or use information from outside the material shown. This is an ex ante judgment: predict which response is more likely to change the OP's view without knowing what actually happened afterward. If useful, you may consider rhetorical features such as credibility, emotional appeal, clarity, appropriateness, and arrangement. These are guidance, not a checklist, and they do not define the answer. Other aspects of the response may also matter. Cogency may contribute to rhetorical effectiveness, but do not simply repeat your cogency judgment. Do not judge whether you would be persuaded.
effectiveness.short: Which response is more likely to change this particular OP's stated view? Use the context available in the OP's post, including reasonable inferences from what the OP says, and make your best prediction. Optional cues include credibility, emotional appeal, clarity, appropriateness, and arrangement; these are guidance, not separate criteria.
effectiveness.question: Which response is more likely to change this particular OP's stated view?

evidence.title: EVIDENTIAL SUPPORT
evidence.full: Evidence is concrete supporting information offered for a claim. It may include facts, data, statistics, research findings, documented real-world examples, or information attributed to an identifiable source. A bare assertion, opinion, value judgment, rhetorical question, insult, or simple restatement of a conclusion does not count as evidence by itself. First, indicate independently whether each response provides any concrete supporting information beyond a bare assertion, opinion, or restatement. If both responses provide evidence, compare their evidential support. Consider how specific and concrete the evidence is, how well it supports the claim being made, and, where relevant, whether the response identifies the source or basis of the evidence. Do not open links, search for sources, or independently fact-check claims. A citation or institutional source is not automatically stronger evidence.
evidence.short: First decide independently whether A and B provide concrete information in support of their arguments. If both do, compare how specific and concrete the evidence is, how well it supports the claim being made, and, where relevant, whether the response identifies the source or basis of the evidence. Do not open links or independently verify the claims.
evidence.presence_question: Which responses provide evidence in support of their argument? Check all that apply.
evidence.comparison_question: Which response provides stronger evidential support for its argument?

unusual_responses: Some randomly sampled responses may be questions, jokes, insults, simple agreement or disagreement, bare assertions, or otherwise provide little argumentative content. This is expected. At the bottom of every annotation screen there are optional checkboxes labeled A: Nonargumentative, B: Nonargumentative, A: Unreadable / truncated, and B: Unreadable / truncated. Check Nonargumentative only when that response clearly provides no supporting reason or argumentative contribution. Check Unreadable / truncated only when the text itself cannot reasonably be evaluated. A flag does not replace the annotation: make the requested judgments as best you can.

examples.title: Example 1 — Cogency
examples.post: CMV: Campus dining does not need to stay open after 8 p.m. because students can simply eat earlier.
examples.a: Some required evening classes end after 8 p.m. Students on meal plans may therefore lose access to food they have already paid for.
examples.b: Campus dining should stay open later because 8 p.m. is too early, and many students probably prefer eating later anyway.
examples.lesson: Response A may be more cogent because its reasons are directly relevant to the conclusion and provide clearer support for it. The example illustrates the cogency criteria; real annotations may be less clear-cut.

examples.title: Example 2 — Expected Rhetorical Effectiveness
examples.post: CMV: I do not use two-factor authentication because I do not want to enter another code every time I log in.
examples.a: Two-factor authentication adds an extra step, but the added security is worth the inconvenience because it makes accounts much harder to compromise.
examples.b: Many services can remember a trusted device, so you may not need a code every time. That directly addresses the inconvenience you are worried about.
examples.lesson: Response B may be more likely to change this particular OP's stated view because it directly addresses the concern the OP identified. In many real annotations, you will need to make your best prediction from the contextual information in the OP's post. The task is not which response would persuade people in general.

examples.title: Example 3 — Evidential Support: evidence present versus absent
examples.post: CMV: My local bus service seems reliable enough.
examples.a: The bus system is unreliable because everyone who uses Route 18 knows that buses are late all the time.
examples.b: The city's 2025 transit report says Route 18 arrived more than five minutes late on 27% of recorded trips.
examples.lesson: Response A makes an empirical claim but provides no concrete supporting information, so its evidence box would remain unchecked. Response B provides a specific statistic and identifies its source, so its evidence box would be checked. You do not need to verify the report.

examples.title: Example 4 — Evidential Support: both responses contain evidence
examples.post: CMV: Route 18 is reliable enough that occasional delays are not a real problem.
examples.a: A local group called Transit Riders for Better Service surveyed 52 people at its 'Fix Our Buses' meeting. Forty-six said Route 18 is frequently late.
examples.b: The city transit agency's automatic vehicle records show that Route 18 arrived more than five minutes late on 29% of 8,412 recorded trips during the last six months.
examples.lesson: Both responses provide evidence, so both evidence boxes would be checked. Response A gives concrete survey results, but the respondents are a small, self-selected group attending a meeting specifically about bus problems. Response B may provide stronger evidential support for a general claim about Route 18's reliability because it directly summarizes thousands of recorded trips over an extended period. The task is to judge how well the evidence presented supports the claim, not to verify either source externally.

references: Johnson & Blair (2006); Blair (2012); Wachsmuth et al. (2017) for cogency and argument-quality structure.
Wachsmuth et al. (2017) and recipient-sensitive persuasion literature for rhetorical-effectiveness guidance.
Wachsmuth et al. (2017) and related evidence-annotation work for evidential-support guidance.
